openers.cryogenian-period: The Cryogenian is the age when the planet nearly froze solid. It opened with magma flooding more than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland, and soon after came a worldwide glaciation that lasted some 57 million years. The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that the surface froze nearly completely, twice, in the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations. Yet life did not stop. Shelled amoebae, sponges and seaweeds appear in these rocks, and red and green algae took over the ocean plankton.
openers.ediacaran-period: The Ediacaran begins at a layer of limestone laid directly on top of the last great glacial deposits. What follows is a world in motion: mountains rose in Antarctica, Australia and the Baltic Shield, and the Pan-African orogeny welded continents into Gondwana. A mantle plume pushed Laurentia and Baltica apart and opened the Iapetus Ocean. By about 600 Ma enough oxygen had built up to form an ozone layer. In the rocks of South China appear embryo-like animals and some of the oldest large, complex fossils known.

reviews.cryogenian-period: The Cryogenian ties volcanoes to ice and ice to life. The Franklin province's fresh basalt drew down carbon dioxide, and glaciation began barely a million or so years later. The Sturtian ice lasted some 57 million years, a relatively warm interval followed, and then the Marinoan brought the last major snowball. Through it all, sponges survived, testate amoebae appeared, seaweeds grew in a short glacial pause, and red and green algae took over the plankton they would rule until the Permian extinction.

prot-110.title: Franklin magma floods the Arctic and cools the world
prot-110.text: More than 1.1 million km² of the Canadian Arctic and northwestern Greenland vanished under magma in about two million years. The Franklin Large Igneous Province, a vast outpouring of basalt lava, ranks among the largest magmatic episodes in Earth's history. Uranium-lead dating puts its rapid emplacement at about 719.9 and 718.6 Ma. Together with the Irkutsk province in Siberia, it marks where Siberia rifted away from Laurentia. Its effect on climate was swift. As fresh basalt weathered, it drew carbon dioxide out of the air, and glaciation began just 0.9–1.6 million years after the lava cooled.

prot-112.title: The Sturtian: fifty-seven million years of ice
prot-112.text:
Ice at or below sea level, on a continent near the equator: that is the evidence that the Sturtian glaciation was global. Lasting from about 717 to 660 Ma, some 57 million years, it was the first of the Cryogenian's great ice ages and the longest and most severe known glaciation after the Huronian. The supercontinent Rodinia then straddled the equator, yet its glaciers reached the shore.

The cold arrived only 0.9–1.6 million years after {{ref:prot-110}} erupted. One explanation joins the two: weathering of fresh basalt pulled carbon dioxide from the air, while Rodinia's breakup left mid-ocean ridges releasing little of it. In the snowball episodes, ice may have covered all but the highest mountains, with average temperatures near −50 °C.

How far the ice reached is still debated. It may have been a Snowball Earth, with ice at very low latitudes, or several regional glaciations; some researchers argue for a slushball with open water at the equator. That the glaciation happened is not in dispute.

prot-111.title: Snowball Earth: did the whole planet freeze
prot-111.text:
Glacial deposits laid down in the tropics turn up on every continent. Glaciers once reached sea level near the equator. From this comes the Snowball Earth hypothesis: that Earth's surface froze nearly completely, most often linked to the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations of the Cryogenian.

Not everyone accepts the full freeze. The glaciation itself is accepted, but scientists still dispute whether ice covered the whole planet or left a slushball, with an open band of water around the equator. Either way, life struggled. Thick ice blocking sunlight would have severely hindered primary production, the growth of algae and other organisms that make food from light, in shallow seas.

The trigger is thought to lie in Rodinia's breakup. The same breakup is linked to the rapid evolution that followed in the Ediacaran and Cambrian, so the frozen world sits right before the great burst of complex life.

prot-113.title: Shelled amoebae appear in the ice age
prot-113.text: Single cells began building houses around 700 Ma. Fossils of testate amoebae, or Arcellinida, single-celled organisms with shells, first appear then, in the middle of the Cryogenian. They were not alone. Porter (2000) suggests red and green algae, stramenopiles, ciliates and dinoflagellates also evolved during this period, so the ice age was a time of new microbial branches.

prot-115.title: A warm pause between two snowballs
prot-115.text: Between the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations came a relatively warm interval. Seas rose and the oceans were anoxic, short of dissolved oxygen. Global biodiversity stayed very low. Oxygen may have reached about 50% of present levels, though chromium isotopes suggest oxygenation was slow and subdued, a lull in the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event.

prot-114.title: Island arcs crash into Gondwana's northern edge
prot-114.text: As the Sturtian glaciers retreated, chains of volcanic islands began colliding with the margin of future Gondwana. The collisions laid down the terranes, crustal blocks, of Avalonia, Armorica and Iberia. An Andean-type volcanic arc formed about 650–600 Ma. Behind it a basin opened 590–560 Ma and closed again 545–540 Ma, while the Avalonian belt struck Gondwana around 650 Ma.

prot-116.title: Algae seize the ocean's plankton
prot-116.text:
Algae multiplied a hundred to a thousandfold. About 659–645 Ma, red and green algae replaced planktonic cyanobacteria as the main marine phytoplankton, the drifting organisms at the base of the ocean food web. Unicellular algae diversified rapidly, and they kept that role until the Permian extinction.

The change rippled upward. Late in the Cryogenian, heterotrophic plankton appeared, drifting organisms that fed on algae and prokaryotes rather than making their own food. Bacteria had ruled the oceans for ages; now their dominance was over.

prot-117.title: Sponges survive the snowball
prot-117.text:
Sponges came through the Cryogenian glaciations alive. They had emerged in the Tonian, and demosponges appear around 650 Ma, building skeletons of spicules, tiny struts made of spongin protein and silica.

The oldest fossils are another matter. Some researchers argue that the oldest sponge fossils, and so the oldest animal fossils, are Cryogenian. Others think they may be proto-sponges or microbial structures, and the question is unsettled. Even the oldest sponge spicules, about 580 Ma from China's Doushantuo Formation and Mongolia, are challenged. Sponges that are unmistakably sponges, such as the non-mineralized Helicolocellus, appear only in the latest Ediacaran.

prot-118.title: Songluo seaweeds in a break from the ice
prot-118.text: In a short break in the Marinoan glaciation, around 650 Ma, large seaweeds grew in what is now South China. These macroalgae fossils form the Songluo Biota. It is the only known macrofossil biota from the Cryogenian, the first large carbonaceous fossils found in rocks of that age.

prot-119.title: The Marinoan, the last great snowball
prot-119.text:
The Marinoan glaciation is described as the most significant snowball Earth event, global in scope. Also called the Varanger or Elatina glaciation, it came late in the Cryogenian. Diamictites, jumbled glacial rubble, record it in South Australia's Adelaide Geosyncline. Its timing is poorly constrained; a 2025 study dates it to 639–635 Ma.

The thaw came from the planet's own chemistry. Volcanic carbon dioxide and dissolving clathrates, gas trapped in ice, ended it, perhaps hastened by methane from permafrost near the equator. It was the last major snowball. Later ice ages covered less of the planet.

prot-120.title: Cap carbonates seal the last snowball
prot-120.text:
Glacial rubble, then suddenly limestone. Across the world, Neoproterozoic glacial deposits are commonly capped by a sharply overlying layer of precipitated limestone or dolomite, metres to tens of metres thick. The Ediacaran Period itself begins at one: the Nuccaleena Formation, directly above Elatina glacial deposits in South Australia's Flinders Ranges.

A favored explanation runs like this. After a snowball, carbon-dioxide-rich acid rain weathered rock and washed calcium into the sea, where it settled as carbonate layers. The glacial link is questioned, though: some caps are too thick for a rapid thaw, and many glacial sequences lack them. The boundary also marks the start of a distinctive pattern of carbon-isotope changes.

prot-121.title: Big, spiny microfossils replace the old plankton
prot-121.text: Plankton that had changed little for ages largely died out as the Ediacaran began. Larger, shorter-lived acritarchs, microfossils of uncertain origin, replaced them. From 635 to about 575 Ma, ornamented forms usually over 100 μm across dominated. They largely vanish before 560 Ma, about when the Ediacara biota arose. If they were animal resting stages, they fit the frequent anoxia of the Ediacaran.

prot-122.title: Beardmore mountains rise in Antarctica
prot-122.text: From about 633 to 620 Ma, the Beardmore orogeny built mountains in Antarctica. It reflects Rodinia's final breakup. The supercontinent's fragments had begun moving back together, toward a new assembly, Pannotia.

prot-123.title: The Petermann orogeny raises the rocks of Uluru
prot-123.text: Uluru owes its rise to a collision far away. Between 630 and 520 Ma, the Petermann orogeny deformed central Australia's Musgrave basement and Amadeus Basin sediments, mountain building in the middle of a continent. Its belt runs unusually east to west, suggesting India struck Western Australia from the northwest as Gondwana assembled. It thrust up the rocks that now form Uluru, laid down around 550–530 Ma.

prot-124.title: Tidal layers record a 21.9-hour day
prot-124.text: About 620 Ma a day lasted 21.9 ± 0.4 hours, and a year held about 400 days and 13.1 lunar months. The record comes from tidal rhythmites, layers of sand and silt laid down off estuaries with strong tides, which preserve daily, monthly and seasonal cycles. Tides slow Earth's spin as the Moon recedes. Since then the Moon has moved away an average of 2.17 cm a year, about half today's rate.

prot-125.title: The Timanide orogeny, Precambrian's last mountain belt
prot-125.text: From about 620 to 550 Ma, the Timanide orogeny reshaped the northern Baltic Shield. It is called the last major orogenic event of the Precambrian. Around 555 Ma, Baltica's northern margin turned active and gathered in new crust: the Timan-Pechora Basin, the northern Urals and Novaya Zemlya.

prot-126.title: Weng'an: embryos turned to stone
prot-126.text: Embryo-like animals, preserved in three dimensions, lie in calcium phosphate in China's Weng'an biota, 609–570 Ma. Its richest layer postdates the Gaskiers glaciation. The rocks belong to the Doushantuo Formation, which spans about 635–551 Ma and bridges the poorly known time between the Cryogenian and the Avalon explosion. Among its finds is Caveasphaera, a 609-million-year-old multicellular organism that may record one of the earliest steps in animal evolution.

prot-127.title: Lantian: seaweeds and possible cnidarians
prot-127.text: Some of the oldest large, complex fossils known come from the Lantian Biota of South China, dated by the rhenium-osmium method to 602 ± 7 Ma. It includes macroalgae and fossils that may be cnidarian-grade animals. Even older macrofossils, the Ancanping assemblage of about 620–610 Ma, occur in the Doushantuo Formation.

prot-128.title: A mantle plume splits Laurentia from Baltica
prot-128.text:
A plume of hot mantle rock, the Central Iapetus Magmatic Province, forced Laurentia and Baltica apart and opened the Iapetus Ocean between them. Rifting began with the Egersund dike swarm in Norway around 650 Ma. From 600 Ma the two continents rotated by up to 180°.

The ocean opened in stages. Its eastern part opened around 590 Ma, and its southern arm, between Laurentia and South America, about 550 Ma. The Tornquist Sea, between Avalonia and Baltica, probably formed at the same time. Bordered by Laurentia, Baltica, Avalonia and other continents, the Iapetus lasted from about 600 to 425 Ma in the Southern Hemisphere.

prot-129.title: The ozone shield goes up
prot-129.text: Sunlight was dangerous before about 600 Ma. Until then, any life on land probably needed other chemicals to screen out ultraviolet radiation. Atmospheric oxygen stood between 1% and 18% of present levels at 800 Ma. Around 600 Ma it began rising more significantly, and enough had accumulated to form an ozone layer, the high gas that filters ultraviolet light.

prot-130.title: The Pan-African orogeny welds Gondwana together
prot-130.text:
Africa was built in collisions. The Pan-African orogeny, a series of major mountain-building events, assembled the supercontinents Gondwana and Pannotia about 600 Ma.

It began around 635 Ma, when the West African and Saharan cratons, the old stable cores of continents, collided and closed the Pharusian Ocean. By about 600 Ma most of western Gondwana had joined, though Australia and East Antarctica were still separate. All the African cratons were in place by about 550 Ma.

The result lasted. Gondwana remained one landmass from about 600 Ma until Pangaea broke up in the Early Jurassic.

prot-131.title: Pannotia, a supercontinent that may never have been
prot-131.text:
Pannotia may have been a supercontinent for only about 50 million years. Also called Greater Gondwana, it is proposed to have formed around 600 Ma during the Pan-African orogeny. It broke up about 560 Ma as the Iapetus Ocean opened, with Laurentia rifting from South America around 565 Ma.

Whether it ever fully existed is debated. A 2022 paper argues it began breaking apart before it was fully assembled. Its breakup, real or partial, came with rising seas, dramatic changes in climate and ocean chemistry, and rapid animal diversification.

prot-132.title: The Acraman impact strikes South Australia
prot-132.text:
About 590 Ma, a chondritic impactor, a stony meteorite, struck what is now the Gawler Ranges of South Australia. The age comes from its ejecta in nearby basins. The crater has eroded, and estimates of its original size range from 35–40 km to 85–90 km. The larger figure implies an explosion of 5.2 million megatons of TNT.

Its debris travelled far. An ejecta layer with shocked minerals and an iridium anomaly lies in Flinders Ranges rocks at least 300 km east. Just above that layer begins a radiation of acritarch microorganisms, and some authors suspect a link.

prot-134.title: Cnidarians: the first animals everyone accepts
prot-134.text: The earliest widely accepted animal fossils look surprisingly modern. They are cnidarians, possibly about 580 Ma, though the Doushantuo fossils are only roughly dated. Their presence means the cnidarian and bilaterian lineages had already split well over 580 Ma. Animals may be older still. Microfossils from 632.5 Ma, just after the Cryogenian ice, may be embryonic resting stages of the earliest known animals.

prot-133.title: The Damara orogeny closes the Adamastor Ocean
prot-133.text: Between 580 and 550 Ma the Damara orogeny stitched the Congo–São Francisco and Río de la Plata cratons together, forming northern Gondwana with India. The Adamastor Ocean closed from north to south, from the Araçuaí Belt to the Kaoko Belt. In Brazil, the Ribeira Belt collision did most of its deformation 590–563 Ma.

prot-135.title: Gaskiers, a short and sharp ice age
prot-135.text:
In about 250,000 years, 579.88–579.63 Ma, glacial deposits formed across eight paleocontinents, some at only 10–30° latitude. This was the Gaskiers glaciation, the last major glacial event of the Proterozoic. It was the shortest of at least three Neoproterozoic ice ages, and unlike the Sturtian and Marinoan, probably not a Snowball Earth.

Its deposits lie just below some of the oldest Ediacaran fossils, though a 9-million-year gap separates them. A proposed scheme would place the base of an Upper Ediacaran series at this glaciation.

prot-136.title: The Avalon explosion: big life arrives
prot-136.text:
Some 36 million years before the Cambrian explosion, life got big. A proposed burst of evolution about 575 Ma, named for fossils on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, is thought to have produced the Ediacaran biota. These were large, mostly soft-bodied organisms, often fixed in place, shaped like tubes and fronds. They are the earliest known complex multicellular life.

The diversity of metazoans, many-celled animals, rose quickly, and the first cnidarians and bilaterians joined them. Yet the newcomers are hard to classify. Their place in the tree of life is unclear, and it is not even established that most of them were animals.

The explosion's definition is itself contested. A 2008 analysis of shape diversity gave the event its name, and that analysis has been disputed; the Ediacaran biota itself is not. Most of these organisms died out in the end-Ediacaran extinction about 539 Ma.

prot-137.title: The Shuram excursion, carbon's biggest swing
prot-137.text:
The largest negative carbon-13 excursion in Earth's history took 50 million years to recover. The Shuram excursion is a shift in the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 in Ediacaran rocks, first noticed in South Australia's Wonoka Formation. Its timing is debated: it began around 573 Ma and ended around 562 or 551 Ma. Diagenesis, chemical change after burial, may exaggerate it.

No one knows what caused it. The oxygen-using Ediacaran biota radiated during it, apparently exploiting a surplus of oxidants, and it may have helped spark the rise of animals that led to the Cambrian explosion.

prot-138.title: Charnia, the fossil that opened the Precambrian
prot-138.text: Charnia was the first Precambrian fossil recognized as such, found in England's Charnwood Forest. It was a frond, with leaf-like ridges branching alternately from a zig-zag midline, living on deep sea floors 570–550 Ma. It is among the most iconic Ediacaran forms, and among the hardest to place in the tree of life.

prot-139.title: The first burrows: animals start to move
prot-139.text:
Something began crawling about 575–560 Ma. Mobile organisms left the earliest trails, moving on and just beneath the microbial mats that carpeted the sea floor. These Ediacaran traces are simple, near-horizontal feeding trails. The first widely accepted burrows come from the lower Blueflower Formation, about 567.3 Ma.

The movers grew more complex. Bilaterians, animals with a left and right side, were present by 555 Ma. By 551 Ma an animal with leg-like appendages was leaving tracks in mud.

prot-140.title: Mistaken Point: a deep-sea community under ash
prot-140.text: Volcanic ash buried the sea floor at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, and preserved its life in fine detail. The ash dates the fossils to 565 ± 3 Ma. The site holds one of the most diverse and best-preserved collections of Precambrian fossils. It defines the deep-water Avalon assemblage, the oldest locality rich in Ediacaran fossils, some of which survive to the base of the Cambrian.

prot-141.title: A failing magnetic field and a young inner core
prot-141.text: Rocks formed about 565 Ma record a geomagnetic field that was unusually weak and pointed in two distinct directions. Reversals were frequent then. One reading is that Earth's solid inner core was only beginning to form, an idea that new Cambrian data appear to support. A 2016 dynamo model predicted a weak field from 1.0 to 0.6 Ga and a strong one after the core began to freeze. The inner core's age remains unresolved, with estimates from 0.5 to 2 billion years.

prot-142.title: The earliest possible arthropods
prot-142.text: Arthropods, the jointed-legged animals, may date to about 560 Ma. Ediacaran forms such as Spriggina, Parvancorina and Yilingia have been interpreted as arthropods, though the link is debated, especially for Parvancorina. Embryos 543 million years old suggest that aspects of arthropod development arose in the late Proterozoic.

prot-143.title: White Sea and Ediacara Hills: crowded sea floors
prot-143.text: One bed on Russia's White Sea coast holds the highest diversity of Ediacaran fossils found, with real ecological complexity. The White Sea biota flourished from 560 to 550 Ma. In South Australia, the Ediacara Hills, the type locality that names the period, preserve abundant fossils of about 555 Ma, like a community of the same age in Sonora, Mexico.

prot-144.title: Dickinsonia, a quilted disc that left trails
prot-144.text: Dickinsonia was a large, slow-moving disc with a quilted surface, first appearing about 558 Ma. In 2018, cholesterol found in its fossils was taken as evidence that it was an early animal, though the molecule may instead point to fungi or red algae. Its fossils often lie at the end of trails matching its shape, perhaps left while it fed.

prot-145.title: Kimberella grazes the sea floor
prot-145.text: Kimberella left scratch marks, perhaps from a radula, a rasping tongue, beside a grazing trail called Kimberichnus. It crawled and fed on the sea floor from about 555 Ma. Some call it mollusc-like; others say only that it was probably a bilaterian with three tissue layers. If it was mollusc-like, the two great branches of bilaterian animals split well before 550 Ma.

prot-146.title: Dengying: the last snapshot before the Phanerozoic
prot-146.text: Several sites in China's Dengying Formation, dated 551–543 Ma, preserve life just before the Phanerozoic. The Jiangchuan biota is dominated by giant thallophytes, simple plant-like organisms, but contains animals similar to later Cambrian sites. At Gaojiashan, fossils turned to pyrite record how the tubes of Cloudina grew.
